**The attention mask determines what a token can see.** Encoder-only models typically let tokens attend bidirectionally across the input, making them effective at building a representation of a complete text. Decoder-only models use causal attention, predicting the next token from the preceding context. Encoder–decoder models encode an input bidirectionally and generate an output through a causal decoder that can also attend to the encoder. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683)

**Match architecture to task.** For classifying a finished review or embedding a document, having access to words on both sides can help. For open-ended generation, next-token prediction naturally supports producing one token after another. For translation or summarization, an encoder–decoder explicitly separates source understanding from target generation.

**Why decoder-only became prominent.** One next-token objective works across text, code, instructions, and many serialized tasks, and large-scale training/serving ecosystems developed around it. This is a practical convergence of data, objectives, scaling, and infrastructure, not proof that bidirectional encoding is obsolete.

For retrieval, a compact encoder can precompute item/document vectors and create a query vector in one forward pass. Generation-oriented models can also be adapted for embeddings, but their existence does not remove the latency and training advantages of a purpose-built embedding model.

Compare quality, parameter count, input/output lengths, and latency for the actual workload. A family name does not uniquely determine behavior: pooling, training objective, masking, and adaptation can matter as much as whether the backbone was originally called an encoder or decoder.

**Technical details and references.**

Encoder-only models see both left and right context and are well suited to classification, tagging, and pooled retrieval representations. Decoder-only models use a causal mask and learn next-token prediction. Encoder–decoder models encode an input bidirectionally and generate an output with causal decoding plus cross-attention. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805) [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683)

$$p(y\mid x)=\prod_t p(y_t\mid x,y_{<t}).$$

Decoder-only models offer a simple common training/generation objective and flexible prompting at scale; that practical success does not establish universal architectural superiority. A bi-encoder can precompute document vectors and score queries with dot products, avoiding token-by-token generation. [4](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084) Encoder–decoders remain useful when input conditioning and output generation have distinct roles. Compare quality at matched data/compute, latency, context size, and output requirements rather than assuming one architecture wins every task.
